content: Data systems should facilitate seamless data transfer between subnational surveillance units and national surveillance programs. This can be achieved either electronically or by manually transferring data downloaded from subnational programs to the national level. When selecting or developing hardware and software for data management systems, these factors must be carefully considered. The surveillance data management system and its associated database should be capable of recording the date when case report forms are received (in paper or electronic form), the date of data entry or upload, and any updates or edits made to existing records, including sentinel events. Cases missing critical information required for inclusion in the surveillance system should be flagged, enabling surveillance staff to follow up and obtain the missing data. Double data entry and manual comparison of entered data are recommended to minimize errors. Any unresolved discrepancies between case records from multiple sources or invalid data should be addressed by contacting the individual who reported the case or sentinel event and cross-referencing the information with original source documents. Providing feedback to individuals completing case report forms or patient records can improve data quality. This includes regular communication with reporting facilities about the completeness of their data, offering support to improve key sites, and promoting the use of dashboards for public health action. HIV case surveillance systems must distinguish between reports of new cases and updates to previously reported cases. If a report pertains to a previously unreported case, a new record should be created. If it relates to a sentinel event for an existing case, the record should be updated with the new information. Algorithms for matching cases often include patient names, personal identifiers, dates of birth, and sex. Phonetic matching systems, such as the Soundex code, can help identify misspelled names but must be combined with other identifiers for effective matching. Additional variables, such as the date of diagnosis, can enhance the algorithm. Record-matching should be standardized and conducted at both subnational and national levels. Linking surveillance data with external data sources, such as vital statistics, is also necessary to update case records. This is particularly concerning for individuals whose behaviors, such as same-sex relationships, sex work, or drug use, are criminalized. Surveillance systems must prioritize confidentiality and secure data storage to prevent breaches. Each organization in the healthcare system should designate a confidentiality and security officer responsible for protecting patient privacy and data security. Confidentiality and security policies should include written procedures for all staff handling surveillance data, reflecting relevant laws and regulations. Breaches of security policies must be reported immediately, investigated promptly, and addressed with appropriate remedial actions. Staff with access to surveillance data should receive annual training on security and confidentiality. Surveillance systems should collect only the minimum data necessary to achieve program goals and use the highest security standards for data collection, storage, and use. Data should be de-identified for analysis and disseminated in aggregate form to prevent inadvertent identification of individuals. Physical access to areas where confidential data is stored should be restricted, and electronic files should be accessible only to authorized personnel. Secure methods, such as encryption, should be used for data transmission, and paper documents should be shredded when no longer needed. Comprehensive evaluations should be conducted periodically, with at least annual assessments of system processes and data quality. Monitoring should focus on achieving complete, timely, and accurate case reporting. Factors influencing reporting completeness include identifying all reporting sources, educating and communicating with those responsible for reporting, and providing clear instructions for completing and submitting case report forms. Feedback to data collectors and users is essential for maintaining data quality. In countries with limited or non-existent disease reporting systems, implementing HIV case surveillance may involve multiple steps. The Ministry of Health should lead the development and implementation process, with input from relevant stakeholders. A steering committee comprising representatives from various organizations and agencies involved in surveillance and service delivery should oversee the process. A technical working group with expertise in disease surveillance, data management, and HIV services should design the system, procedures, and legal framework for case surveillance. The design of the surveillance system should consider the reporting processes and procedures outlined in this chapter, informed by a situational analysis. The implementation plan should define the roles and responsibilities of programs within the Ministry of Health, including data management, analysis, dissemination, and system performance monitoring. Electronic reporting should only be considered in settings with stable power sources and adequate IT infrastructure. The system should be accessible to authorized personnel, built with modifiable software, and supported by local IT expertise.
